newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices soar, oil and gold also gain.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices soar, oil and gold also gain.

text.p: Coffee prices rose sharply on Tuesday after roaster Folgers Coffee raised its retail prices, signaling more worries about this year's supplies.

"The list price of Folgers coffee generally reflects the price of green coffee sold on the commodity market," Folgers said in a statement after it raised its list price for a standard 13-ounce can of ground coffee by 20 cents to $3.06.
The rise was Folgers' third in the last two months, bringing the total rise since then to 80 cents a can, a 35 percent increase.

"Green coffee prices have been rising since January, and have continued due to a number of factors including reduced crop estimates for the upcoming harvest in Brazil, reduced availability of coffee from Central America and Colombia, and the generally tight supply of arabica beans on the worldwide coffee market," said Folgers, a unit of Procter and Gamble.

Bolstered by Folgers' move, coffee for May delivery on the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York closed 6.15 cents a pound higher at 226.40 cents, just below the 2-1/2 year high of 227.50 cents set in early March.

"With the overall fundamentals, nobody's going to bet on this market going lower," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "The combination of tight stocks and indications of a smaller Colombian crop all point to this market going higher."

Demand from roasters and merchants for coffee continues to draw down available supplies. On Tuesday, the exchange said physical coffee stocks certified for delivery against futures fell another 1,500 bags to 47,103 bags as of April 28.
Each bag contains 132 pounds of coffee.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices also surged, led by a rally in heating oil as market talk circulated that a large commercial firm, Vitol S.A. Inc, would take a sizable delivery of heating oil.

Heating oil for May delivery ended up 2.38 cents a gallon at 58.91 cents. Buoyed by those gains, June crude oil ended 53 cents a barrel higher at $20.44 and May unleaded gasoline up 1.02 cents a gallon at 63.36 cents.

The May heating oil contract expires on Wednesday, and physical supplies of heating oil in the New York Harbor have been tight recently as unseasonably cold weather in the northeastern United States drained refinery stocks.
"There was a lot of talk of a short squeeze because someone may be taking a large delivery," said Nauman Barakat, a trader with Prudential Securities.

Vitol, a privately owned Swiss trading firm, declined to comment on the market talk on Tuesday. But the company is an active market player, delivering 892,000 barrels of crude oil against the May crude oil contract last Thursday.

In a "squeeze," a buyer can stand for delivery of the cash commodity and sellers of futures contracts could be called on to deliver. That concern prompted many "shorts," or traders who had sold, to buy back and cancel their obligation. The rush of "short-covering" in turn drove prices up sharply.

Gold prices ended slightly higher, helped by sharply higher Treasury bond prices and a weaker U.S. dollar after U.S. economic data suggested the Federal Reserve might not raise interest rates again in May, traders said.

"The lower dollar and interest rates today could shift the scenario if the Federal Reserve really does refrain from tightening further, but in the meantime funds are heavily short in gold and the trade is looking for lower prices," said analyst Scott Meyers of Pioneer Futures in New York.

Orders for durable goods in March fell 3.0 percent, the largest drop since last August, while the U.S. employment cost index rose 0.6 percent in the first quarter of the year, less than analysts' average forecast for a rise of 0.9 percent.
Gold for June delivery in New York ended up 20 cents at $341.60 an ounce.

The threat of higher real interest rates and the strong U.S. dollar have been deterring investors from seeing value in precious metals. Fears of further sales of gold by central banks or the International Monetary Fund also continued to hang over the market, traders said.
